docs.text: Beneath the Mesa Assessing Aquifer, Well, and Acequia Water Resources Across Sandoval County, New Mexico ENG 220 · Team 23 Open the live app · View the code on GitHub About the project Water scarcity is a persistent challenge across New Mexico. Sandoval County spans several hydrogeologic settings, and its communities depend on a mix of groundwater wells, surface water, and acequia irrigation systems. This project evaluates the condition and long-term viability of those water resources across the county, with Cuba, New Mexico, on the eastern edge of the San Juan Basin, as a focused case study. The project is motivated by concern about declining groundwater near Cuba, but rather than assume how severe that decline is or what is causing it, we test what the available public data actually show. Approach The study works at two levels: County-wide screening. Map and compare aquifers, wells, water levels, water quality, and acequia and surface-water features across Sandoval County. Because the county crosses several geologic regions, comparisons are grouped by region or aquifer system instead of treating the county as one uniform aquifer. Cuba case study. A closer look at the Ojo Alamo Sandstone and San Jose Formation near Cuba, using San Juan Basin aquifer datasets alongside nearby well, water-level, and water-quality records. The analysis focuses on measurable indicators such as depth to water, water-level change over time, well depth, aquifer unit, and salinity, rather than a full hydrologic model. Where records are sparse, the results say so instead of filling the gaps. Research questions How do groundwater levels vary across Sandoval County, and which areas show sustained decline, stability, or recovery? What do well records show about well depth, depth to water, and the aquifer units that communities rely on? Do the available data support the concern that Cuba's main groundwater source is approaching severe depletion? How do the Ojo Alamo Sandstone and San Jose Formation compare near Cuba in extent, thickness, hydraulic properties, water levels, and water quality? How does groundwater quality, including salinity, vary across the county and near Cuba? Where are acequias located, what surface water do they depend on, and which communities do they serve? Do changes in groundwater levels line up with nearby surface-water or acequia conditions, or are the records too limited to tell? Where is monitoring coverage strong, and where are the most important data gaps? Which indicators can be combined into a dashboard that shows water-resource stress without overstating how certain the data are? How this site is organized The site follows the project's stages, from collecting data to presenting results. Each stage page explains what was done, which files it produced, and who led it. docs.text: 2. Data cleaning Lead: James Wanueka This stage turns the raw downloads into tables the analysis code can use directly. Starting notes What the raw files already need: ose_aquifer_test_wells.csv covers all of New Mexico. Filtering COUNTY NAME to SANDOVAL keeps 179 of its 3,455 records. water_flow_data_sandoval_county_sources.csv mixes ten measurement types, each in its own units (cubic feet per second, feet, mg/L, and so on). Split it by parameter_code before comparing values. The same file mixes monthly, calendar-year, and water-year periods ( interval_type ) and several statistics per period ( parent_statistic_name : mean, minimum, maximum, median). Pick one combination per chart so values aren't double counted. Cleaning steps To be written: each step, in order, and the script that does it. Cleaned outputs To be written: the cleaned files this stage produces and where they're saved. Problems and decisions To be written: missing values, odd records, and how they were handled.

docs.text: 1. Data collection Lead: Dylan Gonzales This stage covers finding public datasets that can answer the research questions , downloading them, and recording where each one comes from. Datasets in the repository water_flow_data_sandoval_county_sources.csv USGS monthly and yearly statistics for 30 monitoring sites in Sandoval County (17 stream gages, 9 wells, 2 canals, and 2 reservoirs), with records from 1926 to 2026. Covers streamflow, depth to groundwater, reservoir storage, suspended sediment, water temperature, and water-quality measures: specific conductance, dissolved oxygen, pH, and turbidity. Source: To be added: link to the page this file was downloaded from. ose_aquifer_test_wells.csv New Mexico Office of the State Engineer aquifer-test records, 3,455 statewide and 179 in Sandoval County, including well depth, screened interval, geologic formation, and hydraulic properties such as transmissivity and storativity. Source: To be added: link to the page this file was downloaded from. Why these datasets To be written: why each dataset was chosen and which research questions it helps answer. Still to collect The proposal also calls for the following data, which isn't in the repository yet: Aquifer geometry near Cuba: USGS San Juan Basin digital aquifer data for the Ojo Alamo Sandstone and San Jose Formation. Water quality and salinity: the NM Bureau of Geology San Juan Basin Brackish Water Assessment and New Mexico Water Data records. Acequias: locations and service areas of acequias and community ditches from the NM Interstate Stream Commission. More water-level records: National Ground-Water Monitoring Network and Healy Collaborative Groundwater Monitoring Network data, to add wells beyond the 9 in the USGS file. Shallow groundwater depth: the mean annual depth to groundwater for the shallow riparian aquifer dataset. County boundary: a Sandoval County boundary layer to organize the maps. Sources USGS San Juan Basin digital aquifer data (ScienceBase) USGS groundwater-flow model report, WRI 95-4187 NM Bureau of Geology: San Juan Basin Brackish Water Assessment New Mexico Office of the State Engineer National Ground-Water Monitoring Network Healy Collaborative Groundwater Monitoring Network New Mexico Water Data Catalog NM Interstate Stream Commission: Acequias

docs.text: Findings Results will be added here as the analysis is completed. Following the proposal, each finding is labeled as one of these: Measured: a trend or pattern the data show directly. Hypothesis: a possible explanation the data are consistent with but don't prove. Insufficient data: a question the available records can't answer yet. Sections will cover groundwater levels, wells and aquifer units, the Cuba case study, water quality, acequias and surface water, and data gaps.
